newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BT sows up Europe with French deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BT sows up Europe with French deal.

text.p: British Telecommunications (BT) said on Thursday that a 1.1 billion pound ($1.7 billion) investment in France had secured its position as a pan-European telecom player and dismissed criticism that it was a gamble.

The company is taking a 25 percent stake in a new, four billion pound French telecom group, CEGETEL, which it hopes will become the main rival to state-owned France Telecom when the French market is opened up to competition in 1998.

BT, which already has operations in 30 countries and employs about 130,000 staff world-wide, is also investing the share capital of BT France, worth about 100 million francs ($19.4 million), in the venture with France's Compagnie Generale des Eaux.
Analysts welcomed the news that secures BT's presence in France with one of the best partners available -- and knocks out its major rival in Europe, U.S. telecom giant AT&T.

"Compagnie Generale des Eaux (CGE), is the only major company in France that has made serious noises about wanting to compete with France Telecom," said a London-based telecoms analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The deal, which BT said would be marginally earnings dilutive in the short term but was expected to have "significant long-term benefits", comes on top of BT's alliances in Spain, Italy, Germany, France, Holland and Scandinavia.

"It now gives us enough reach that we can call ourselves pan-European," said Sir Peter Bonfield, BT's chief executive. "We can gain economies of scale across Europe with billing systems and technology."
Bonfield dismissed criticism that BT was paying over the odds in a desperate attempt to gain access to the French telecom market, estimated to be worth about 14.8 billion pounds.
"It's not short-term desperation, it's long-term planning," he told a news conference, adding that talks between the two companies had been "short and mostly sweet".
"It is a lot of money but I think it is a fair price," he said. BT said it would be disappointed if it did not gain access to 15-20 percent of the French telecoms market.

BT is hoping that CEGETEL, which has not yet traded and currently has only mobile telephone interests, will next year win a fixed licence to operate a full range of telephony services in France from 1998.

BT now says it is well-placed to become the second operator in major European countries ahead of market liberalisation in 1998. But Bonfield said it was too soon for BT to switch its focus away from this continent and towards key Asian markets.

As there is no magic January 1, 1998 date for competition in Asian telephone markets, Bonfield said BT -- which already has a joint venture in Japan, the world's second-largest telecom market -- would be seeking alliances there "country by country".

BT and CGE, which is taking a 50 percent stake in CEGETEL, are teaming up with American's SBC Communications Inc, formerly South Western Bell, which is taking a 15 percent stake, and Germany's Mannesmann, which is taking 10 percent.

CEGETEL's principle asset is its 76.8 percent stake in loss-making SFR, France's number two mobile telephone group. SFR says it has won about 40 percent of the mobile telecom market, with over 700,000 subscribers.

The company, which posted a pretax loss of 769 million francs in 1995, is not expected to move into profit before 1998 and has been criticised for not investing soon enough in GSM (global system for mobile communications) technology.

Britain's mobile telephone operator Vodafone Group has a 20 percent stake in SFR. Alcatel Alsthom Cie Generale d'Electricite' is selling its indirect holding in the French company as part of the deal.
BT's shares were trading at a steady 364.5p, up two pence. ($1=.6416 Pound) ($1=5.145 French Franc)
